evidence_quotes.quote: The approach used to elicit information on household preferences with regard to improving system reliability is a survey based contingent valuation (CV) method that uses stated preference behavior (i.e. WTP) to gauge support for changes in the provision of publicly provided goods
To complement the CV analysis, households were also asked to choose between ENACAL and the municipality of León as potential providers of water services

The law of municipalities (article 7) assigns the responsibility for providing water services to municipalities, including building, operating, and maintaining water infrastructure. In practice, however, the implementation of decentralization initiatives is in the initial stages, with only 26 (out of 152) municipalities推进

A stratified random sampling strategy was followed to select a representative sample of urban households from a tax assessment map of León. A total of 690 surveys were completed with the in-person interview process for a response rate of 74 %

The CV scenario started by presenting the characteristics of the existing water system, followed by an improvement in the water system reliability (no interruptions). The water quality and service provider varied according to the experimental design.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household piped drinking-water supply in León, Nicaragua, focusing on intermittent water supply coping strategies and household valuation of uninterrupted (24 h/day) drinking-water service.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — investigates household preferences regarding water service governance/decentralization (centralized national utility ENACAL vs. municipal government provision, contextualized by Article 7 of Nicaragua's Law of Municipalities and the 2005-2015 National Water Strategy) and hypothetical monthly service fees in a contingent valuation survey. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — all surveyed households reside in León under the same centralized utility (ENACAL), where municipal decentralization has not been implemented; provider identity (ENACAL vs. municipality) and monthly fees appear solely as hypothetical vignettes in a stated-preference survey rather than an enacted or operating rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical data from an in-person survey of 690 randomly sampled urban households in León, Nicaragua (560 observations in censored logistic regression models and binomial/logit analyses).
criterion_notes.c4: NO — all analyzed outcomes are stated preferences rather than realized service access outcomes: specifically, (1) hypothetical referendum votes and estimated willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a proposed 24-hour water supply upgrade, and (2) subjective perceptions/preferences choosing between ENACAL and the municipality on institutional attributes (perceived capacity, knowledge, interest, accountability, investment). Current daily hours of water supply (mean 19.77 hours) and current water expenditures are reported only as single-city descriptive background/covariates under ENACAL, not as outcomes evaluated across any legal or governance factor. Comparing hypothetical median WTP to an OECD 3% income benchmark reflects stated demand valuation, not actual tariff unaffordability or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (urban households/respondents in León, Nicaragua; n = 690 surveyed, n = 560 in regressions), exposure (randomized 2x2 split-sample contingent valuation vignettes varying hypothetical service provider and water quality, plus randomized monthly fee bids), outcome (hypothetical referendum vote / log WTP and stated institutional preference), and study design (cross-sectional contingent valuation survey with split-sample experimental treatments) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Cross-sectional household contingent valuation (stated-preference) survey with a randomized 2x2 split-sample experimental vignette design, analyzed via censored logistic regression and binomial/logit tests.
population_and_sample: Urban households in León, Nicaragua (unit of analysis: household/respondent; stratified random sample of 690 completed in-person household interviews from a tax assessment map, 74% response rate; 560 observations in WTP regression models).
exposure: Hypothetical 2x2 split-sample contingent valuation treatments varying proposed water service provider (centralized national utility ENACAL vs. decentralized Municipality of León) and proposed water quality (existing quality vs. safe drinking water), alongside randomly assigned hypothetical monthly fees (C$ 100 to C$ 600) and household covariates including home ownership.
outcome: Stated willingness-to-pay (log WTP / median WTP) derived from hypothetical referendum voting for uninterrupted (24 h/day) tap water service, and stated respondent preference choosing between ENACAL and the municipality across perceived institutional characteristics (service quality, local knowledge, interest, capacity, accountability, investment).
rationale: Exclude as E04 (Wrong outcome). Although the paper addresses urban household drinking-water reliability in León, Nicaragua, and uses a randomized 2x2 contingent valuation vignette comparing centralized (ENACAL) versus municipal governance, its empirical outcomes are exclusively stated preferences — hypothetical referendum votes / willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a proposed 24/7 service upgrade and attitudinal perceptions of institutional competence — rather than realized water access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (c4 = no). Current daily water supply hours and tap-water expenditures are measured only as baseline covariates within a single city served solely by ENACAL. Furthermore, under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2, decentralization in León is presented only as a hypothetical survey scenario rather than an operating rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (plain c2 = yes; narrow c2 = no). Note: statistical non-significance of the provider indicator in the pooled WTP model played no role in this exclusion decision.
